h1: Bugs That Look Like Termites: What Else It Could Be, by Where You Found It
dek: Winged ants at a window, yellow ants rising through a basement crack, booklice on damp paper and beetles boring through floors all get taken for termites. Real photos, the antenna check and where each one turns up.
excerpt: Winged ants, larger yellow ants, carpenter ants, booklice and powderpost beetles get mistaken for termites. Sort yours by where you found it, with real photos.

quickAnswer.lead: **A termite has straight, beaded antennae, a thick waist with no pinch and, if winged, four wings of equal length; each common look-alike fails at least one of those checks.** Ants have elbowed antennae and a pinched waist ([Mississippi State University Extension](https://extension.msstate.edu/insects/termites/are-these-termites-or-ants)), booklice long, threadlike antennae, and beetles a hard shell of wing covers.
bullets: Eastern subterranean termite workers are creamy white, wingless and 1/8 to 1/4 inch long, and the winged ones 3/8 to 1/2 inch, according to [Penn State Extension](https://extension.psu.edu/carpenter-ants).
Carpenter ant workers are shiny, dark brown to black and 1/4 to 1/2 inch long, and winged carpenter ants reach 3/4 inch, Penn State says.

Larger yellow ant swarmers, about 1/4 to 3/8 inch to the wing tips, come up through cracks in basement walls and floors, according to [Ohio State University](https://cfaes.osu.edu/fact-sheet/ants-and-around-home).
Booklice are only about 1/25 to 1/12 inch (1 to 2 mm) long, pale and wingless, says [Colorado State University](https://webdoc.agsci.colostate.edu/bspm/Hexapoda%20%28Insects%29/Booklice.pdf).
Lyctid powderpost beetles are 1/16 to 1/4 inch long and leave round exit holes about the size of a pinhead, says the [University of Kentucky](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef616).

Old house borer larvae grow to about an inch long and tunnel through pine and other softwood framing, and their signs are easiest to find in attics, crawl spaces and unfinished basements, according to [Kentucky's old house borer fact sheet](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef653).

body.text: How can you tell a real termite from a look-alike?

Look at three things: the antennae, the waist and, on a winged insect, the wings. [Purdue Extension](https://extension.entm.purdue.edu/publications/HN-61.pdf) describes winged termites with straight, bead-like antennae, a thick waist and four long wings of equal length, and the [University of Georgia's termite bulletin](https://fieldreport.caes.uga.edu/publications/B1209/) calls the antennae straight to slightly curved. [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/safepestcontrol/termites-how-identify-and-control-them) adds that they may droop, but they do not bend at an angle the way an ant's do.

body.alt: Dark termite swarmers seen from above on a pale wall, each with straight beaded antennae, a thick body with no waist and pale gray wings reaching well past the body
body.caption: Eastern subterranean termite swarmers (Reticulitermes flavipes) on the wall of a metal-sided building in Houston, Missouri, in April 2026, identified on iNaturalist. Look for the straight, beaded antennae, the body with no pinched waist and the wings reaching far past the body.

body.text: Termites without wings follow the same body plan. [Kansas State University's guide to household pests](https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/MF3291.pdf) describes workers as creamy white, soft-bodied, wingless and eyeless, and says they dry out easily, so they stay inside the colony; EPA says termites seldom leave the soil, mud tubes or wood they are tunneling through. A pale insect walking across a shelf or a book is therefore unlikely to be a termite worker.

Swarmers are the termites most people actually see. Purdue puts winged termites at about 1/4 to 3/8 inch, black to yellow-brown, with smoke-gray to brown wings that reach past the body, and Kansas State says the wings lie flat over the back and break off easily after a short flight. The [guide to what termites look like](/blog/what-do-termites-look-like) covers workers, soldiers and swarmers in turn.

body.title: Five checks, with the insect in a jar
items: **Antennae.** Straight and beaded: termite. Bent like an elbow: ant. Long, fine threads on a speck no bigger than 1/12 inch: booklouse.
**Waist.** A termite's body runs straight from front to back with no pinch; an ant is pinched in the middle, like a figure 8.
**Wings.** Four of the same length, longer than the body and quick to fall off: termite. Front pair longer than the hind pair, and firmly attached: ant.
**Shell.** A hard back of wing covers means a beetle; termites are soft-bodied.
**Size and smell.** Measure it against a ruler and compare with the quick-ID table; a winged ant that smells of citronella when crushed is probably a larger yellow ant.

body.text: Are the winged bugs at the window termites or ants?

They can be either, and three checks tell them apart: an ant has elbowed antennae, a pinched waist and front wings longer than its hind wings, where a termite has straight antennae, no waist and four equal wings. The [National Pesticide Information Center](https://npic.orst.edu/pest/termite.html) notes that many ants look very similar to termites and tend to swarm at the same time. [The flying ants vs termites comparison](/blog/flying-ants-vs-termites) takes each check in turn, and [the guide to flying ants](/blog/flying-ants) explains why ants swarm.

If they are termites, take it seriously: Purdue calls winged termites in a home a near-certain sign of infestation and their shed wings a warning, though Kansas State says one or two may simply have fluttered in from outdoors.
What are the winged bugs coming up through the basement floor?

They may be larger yellow ants. [Ohio State University's ant fact sheet](https://cfaes.osu.edu/fact-sheet/ants-and-around-home) says these ants are often mistaken for winged termites, because the winged adults swarm up through cracks in basement walls or floors, crawl around and are drawn to lights. The swarmers are dark brown to blackish-brown with somewhat clouded wings and measure about 1/4 to 3/8 inch to the wing tips; the workers are pale yellowish-brown and 5/32 to 3/16 inch long.

body.alt: Winged reddish-brown ant seen from above on gray woven fabric, with bent antennae and translucent, dark-veined wings folded over its back
body.caption: A winged female larger yellow ant (Lasius interjectus) on fabric in Urbana, Illinois, identified on iNaturalist. Look for the elbowed antennae; a termite's are straight and beaded.

body.text: As ants, they have elbowed antennae and a pinched waist, and Ohio State says they give off a strong smell like citronella when crushed. The colony lives in the soil beside the foundation, under the basement floor, in concrete voids or in rotting wood, and the workers feed on honeydew from aphids and mealybugs on the roots of nearby shrubs.

Other insects rise from below too: [Penn State Extension's pavement ant page](https://extension.psu.edu/pavement-ant) says pavement ants, which nest under sidewalks and building slabs, can swarm at any time of year inside heated buildings, and termites can emerge indoors, so check the antennae and wings of each one.
Is it a carpenter ant or a termite?

A carpenter ant is shiny, dark brown to black and pinched at the waist; a termite worker is creamy white and straight-bodied. [Penn State Extension's carpenter ant page](https://extension.psu.edu/carpenter-ants) says homeowners may mistake one for the other because both live in colonies and excavate wood, and gives carpenter ant workers as 1/4 to 1/2 inch long, with winged ones up to 3/4 inch, against 1/8 to 1/4 inch for eastern subterranean termite workers.

body.alt: A dead black ant curled on its side beside the edge of a metal ruler, its narrow waist and jointed legs visible
body.caption: A dead ant that its photographer identified as a black carpenter ant (Camponotus pennsylvanicus), shown beside a ruler for size. Look for the dark color and the pinched waist, both unlike a pale termite worker.
body.credit: Original uploader was Muéro at en.wikipedia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: Their work in wood differs too. Carpenter ants do not eat wood: Penn State says they dump piles of coarse, stringy wood particles mixed with dead insect parts outside the nest, and that their galleries are smooth-sided, with no soil or fecal pellets. The [USDA Forest Service's Wood Handbook](https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/62262) says they prefer wood that is naturally soft or softened by decay, so finding them can point to a moisture problem, and that in certain regions they can cause as much destruction as termites.
[How to find a carpenter ant nest](/blog/carpenter-ants-canada) walks through the search, and [the carpenter ant bite guide](/blog/do-carpenter-ants-bite) tells carpenter ants from other house ants.
Small ants in old termite damage

Ants in old termite galleries are not necessarily termites coming back. [Clemson's acrobat ant fact sheet](https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/acrobat-ants/) says acrobat ants, 1/16 to 1/8 inch long and black to light brown, may enlarge cavities left by other insects, old termite galleries among them, prefer moist wood softened by decay, and may nest in wall voids and rigid board insulation. The tell is the heart-shaped abdomen, which the ant raises over its thorax and head when disturbed.
What are the tiny pale bugs in books, papers or a damp bathroom?

Booklice. The [Bohart Museum of Entomology at UC Davis](https://bohart.ucdavis.edu/sites/g/files/dgvnsk4616/files/media/documents/note_62_psocids.pdf) describes them as tiny, pale insects that resemble minute termites, wingless and about 1/25 inch (1 mm) long as adults. Colorado State puts them at about 1/25 to 1/12 inch (1 to 2 mm) and says that although they somewhat resemble miniature termites, their long, threadlike antennae set them apart, since a termite's are beaded.

body.alt: A tiny pale brown speck, a booklouse, on a cream page of handwriting just beside the point of a pen
body.caption: A booklouse (genus Liposcelis) on a handwritten page beside a pen tip, in London, identified on iNaturalist. At about 1/25 to 1/12 inch long, it is far smaller than a termite worker.
body.credit: (c) Marco Zaccaria Di Fraia, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: Booklice live on mold, not wood. Colorado State says that indoors they are almost always found in damp places that support the molds they feed on, bathrooms among them, and calls them very minor household pests that cannot bite. [The booklice guide](/blog/booklice) covers them in full, and [the guide to tiny white bugs](/blog/tiny-white-bugs) sorts the other pale specks found indoors.
What is leaving tiny holes and powder in wood floors and furniture?

Usually powderpost beetles, whose larvae bore through wood and leave as hard-shelled adults. The [University of Kentucky](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef616) ranks them second only to termites at damaging dry, seasoned wood, and [University of Missouri Extension](https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g7422) says their feeding tunnels can be told apart from termite and carpenter ant damage.

body.alt: A slender brown beetle with finely ridged, hard wing covers and short segmented antennae, standing on freshly split, splintered wood
body.caption: A European lyctus beetle (Lyctus linearis), one of the powderpost beetles, on split wood, as identified by its photographer. Its hard wing covers set it apart from any termite.
body.credit: Stanislav Snäll, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: Lyctid powderpost beetles are slender, reddish-brown to black and 1/16 to 1/4 inch long, and Kentucky links their infestations with hardwood flooring, paneling, molding, window and door frames and furniture. Their round exit holes are about the size of a pinhead, and the powder sifting out feels like flour or fine talc. Anobiid beetles leave holes 1/16 to 1/8 inch across and gritty powder, and are worst in damp crawl spaces, basements, garages and unheated outbuildings, where Kentucky says they can seriously damage beams and joists.

body.alt: Close-up of a worn wooden floorboard where wear has opened winding beetle tunnels, with a few small round exit holes in the surface
body.caption: Exit holes and larval tunnels of wood-boring beetles, known as woodworm, exposed in a worn floorboard; its photographer did not name the species. Small round holes and winding tunnels with no mud in them point to beetles, not termites.
body.credit: ML5 at English Wikipedia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: The powder and the mud separate beetle work from termite work. [UC IPM's guide to wood-boring beetles in homes](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/wood-boring-beetles-in-homes/) says powderpost frass differs from the larger, granular, almost pepperlike pellets drywood termites leave, which carry ridges on their sides, and the Wood Handbook describes subterranean termite galleries speckled with mud, where powderpost tunnels are packed with fine sawdust. UC IPM adds that the adult beetles fly toward light, so dead ones often turn up on windowsills.

[What termite damage looks like](/blog/termite-damage) sets termite, carpenter ant and beetle damage side by side, and [the guide to beetles in the house](/blog/beetles-in-house) has a pen-tip test for telling powderpost exit holes apart.
Are the white bugs inside the wood termites or beetle grubs?

Look at who is in the tunnels and what fills them. In an active termite colony the mud tunnels are filled with workers, Kansas State says: creamy white, soft-bodied insects that do all the colony's labor. Powderpost galleries are instead packed with powder produced by grub-like larvae, according to Kansas State, and Missouri describes most wood-boring beetle larvae as yellowish white with dark jaws.

body.alt: A cluster of creamy-white, soft, wingless termites crawling over broken, decaying wood and clumps of dark soil
body.caption: Eastern subterranean termites (Reticulitermes flavipes) on decaying wood and soil in New Jersey, identified on iNaturalist; the record does not say which caste they are. Look for the pale, soft bodies with no pinched waist, crowded together.

body.text: In pine framing, a larger grub may be an old house borer. The [University of Kentucky's old house borer fact sheet](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef653) describes mature larvae about an inch long, with black jaws and three tiny dark eyespots in a row on each side of the head, visible with a hand lens. The beetle infests only softwoods such as pine, fir and spruce, most often in houses less than about 10 years old. Its signs are oval exit holes 1/4 to 3/8 inch across, easiest to spot in attics, crawl spaces and unfinished basements, and gnawing sounds from the wood.

body.alt: A cream-white, segmented grub with a dark head end lying on split pale pine wood, below an opened tunnel lined with powdery wood dust
body.caption: An old house borer larva (Hylotrupes bajulus), as identified by its photographer, beside its tunnel in pine wood. Look for the plump, segmented body and the dark head end.
body.credit: Rasbak, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: Ant nests hold pale young. Kansas State describes ant larvae as translucent, white, soft-bodied and legless, cared for by adult workers that carry the ant's elbowed antennae and pinched waist.
Beetles that ride in on firewood

Kansas State says longhorned beetles, whose antennae are as long as or longer than their slender bodies, and shiny, metallic, bullet-shaped wood borers come into homes in firewood, and that the adults, 1/2 to 1 1/2 inches long depending on the species, are often seen around lights and windows; the chance of them emerging from firewood and infesting the house is extremely remote, it adds.
Which termite look-alikes damage wood?
Termites and the beetles feed inside wood, while carpenter ants and carpenter bees dig nest tunnels in it; the Wood Handbook sorts their work by what each leaves behind.

body.text: Carpenter bees are on the list for their holes, not their looks: the Wood Handbook describes large bees that resemble bumblebees but have no hair on the abdomen. [A guide to carpenter bees](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-carpenter-bees-canada) covers the nest holes, and [the termite droppings guide](/blog/termite-droppings) shows drywood termite pellets up close.

body.text: What should you do once you know what it is?
Match the next step to the insect; only termites call for a termite inspection.

items: **Termites.** Save a few insects or wings, check the crawl space, foundation and pipe openings for the mud tubes Kansas State describes, and arrange an inspection. Purdue says swarmers indoors call for a professional pest manager, and EPA says termite firms must be licensed by your state.
**Winged ants.** Find where they came from; [the flying ants guide](/blog/flying-ants) explains what a swarm indoors means.
**Carpenter ants.** Look for the nest and the moisture behind it: Kansas State advises checking wood affected by water seepage, such as window sills, roofs, porch floors, posts and columns.
**Booklice.** Dry the room out: [Penn State Extension's booklice page](https://extension.psu.edu/booklice) says relative humidity below 50% prevents mold growth and booklouse development.

**Powderpost beetles and old house borers.** Make sure the infestation is still active. Kentucky's old house borer fact sheet says fresh powder the color of newly sawn wood points to activity, while powder under dust or cobwebs suggests it has stopped, and both Kentucky fact sheets say a definite diagnosis may need an entomologist or a knowledgeable pest professional.
**Firewood beetles.** Store firewood outdoors and bring in only what you need, as Kansas State advises.

body.title: Bring the bug, not a description
body.text: Seal a few insects or loose wings in a small jar, photograph one beside a ruler marked in inches, and note where and when you found them. Your state's cooperative extension office or a licensed pest professional can identify them from that.

faqs.question: What bug is most often mistaken for a termite?
faqs.answer: Usually winged ants. Kansas State University says winged ants are often mistaken for swarming termites, and the National Pesticide Information Center notes that many ants look very similar to termites and tend to swarm at the same time. Carpenter ants get confused with termites for another reason: Penn State Extension says both live in colonies and excavate wood. Check the antennae, the waist and the wings. Ants have elbowed antennae, a pinched waist and front wings longer than the hind pair; termites have straight antennae, no waist and four equal wings.

faqs.question: What are the white bugs that look like termites?
faqs.answer: Pale, soft, wingless insects crowding damaged wood, soil or mud tubes are most likely termite workers, which Kansas State University describes as creamy white and eyeless. Smaller pale bugs on damp paper or in a bathroom are probably booklice, about 1/25 to 1/12 inch long with long, threadlike antennae, according to Colorado State. A grub-like larva in a tunnel packed with powder is a wood-boring beetle larva; Missouri Extension describes most as yellowish white with dark jaws. White, legless larvae in an ant nest are young ants, Kansas State says.

faqs.question: Do booklice mean you have termites?
faqs.answer: No. Booklice feed on mold and fungi, Penn State Extension says, so a crowd of them points to damp air or damp materials, not to termites. The Bohart Museum at UC Davis notes that these tiny, pale insects resemble minute termites, which is where the mix-up starts, but Colorado State says their long, threadlike antennae tell them apart from a termite's beaded ones. Termite workers stay inside wood, soil or mud tubes. Penn State says keeping relative humidity below 50% prevents booklouse development.

faqs.question: What looks like termite damage but isn't?
faqs.answer: Powderpost beetles, old house borers, carpenter ants and carpenter bees all damage wood. The USDA Forest Service's Wood Handbook sorts them by what they leave: subterranean termite galleries are speckled with mud, carpenter ant galleries are clean and polished, powderpost tunnels are packed with fine sawdust, and carpenter bees bore round holes about 1/2 inch across. The University of Kentucky says lyctid powderpost beetles leave round holes about the size of a pinhead, and old house borers oval holes 1/4 to 3/8 inch across.

faqs.question: How can you tell a termite from an ant without a magnifying glass?
faqs.answer: Look at the color, the wings and where it is. Penn State Extension says carpenter ant workers are shiny, dark brown to black, while eastern subterranean termite workers are creamy white. On winged insects, Ohio State University says termite wings are milky white or grayish, longer than the body and easily shed, while ant wings are clear or brownish and firmly attached, so loose wings of equal size on a sill point to termites. Termite workers also stay hidden inside wood, soil or mud tubes.

faqs.question: Do carpenter ants look like termites?
faqs.answer: Not up close, though the two can be confused. Penn State Extension says homeowners may mistake them because both live in colonies and excavate wood. A carpenter ant worker is shiny, dark brown to black and 1/4 to 1/2 inch long, with a pinched waist and elbowed antennae; an eastern subterranean termite worker is creamy white, 1/8 to 1/4 inch long and straight-bodied. Carpenter ants do not eat wood: they push out coarse shavings, and their galleries are smooth, with no soil.

faqs.question: Why are flying ants coming up through my basement floor?
faqs.answer: They may be larger yellow ants. Ohio State University says these ants live in the soil next to the foundation, under basement floors, in concrete voids or in rotting wood, and that their winged adults swarm up through cracks in basement walls or floors and are drawn to lights, which is why they are often mistaken for winged termites. Ohio State says they give off a strong citronella-like smell when crushed. Check the antennae as well, since termites can also swarm indoors.

faqs.question: Do powderpost beetles look like termites?
faqs.answer: No. They are hard-shelled beetles, slender and reddish-brown to black, 1/16 to 1/4 inch long in the lyctid group, according to the University of Kentucky. The confusion comes from their damage: Kentucky ranks them second only to termites at damaging dry, seasoned wood. Their signs are small round exit holes and powder that feels like flour or fine talc, rather than mud. UC IPM says the adults fly toward light, so dead ones often collect on windowsills.

faqs.question: Are termite look-alikes harmful?
faqs.answer: Some are, in different ways. Carpenter ants, powderpost beetles and old house borers damage wood, and the University of Kentucky says anobiid powderpost beetles can seriously damage beams and joists. Clemson says acrobat ants bite on occasion and sometimes strip the insulation from electrical or telephone wires. Booklice are among the mildest: Colorado State calls them very minor household pests that cannot bite. Larger yellow ants feed on honeydew from aphids and mealybugs on shrub roots, according to Ohio State University.

faqs.question: Do ants and termites swarm at the same time of year?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. The National Pesticide Information Center says many ants tend to swarm at the same time as termites. Kansas State University says termite swarms are most common in spring after the first warm rains, beginning as the day warms, around 10 a.m., and the University of Georgia gives February through April for the eastern subterranean termite, mainly when outdoor temperatures are warm. Some ants break the pattern: Penn State Extension says pavement ants can swarm at any time of year inside heated buildings.
